## TL;DR

Tailnet server discovery now tries a small HTTPS peer endpoint before using the existing SSH path for older servers. The shared implementation remains in `src/core/tailnet-servers.ts`, so the CLI and Hub receive a common result shape. Device filtering now considers OS, tags, and recognizable phone or tablet names, and the Hub groups machine check failures in a collapsed section. I updated the mobile and user-facing discovery documentation. A production tailnet and phone were not available in this session, so no real-device discovery outcome is claimed.

## Work and rationale

The central behavior change is in the shared core collector. It still obtains its peer list from `tailscale status --json`, preserving the stable MagicDNS identity and existing configured-host fallback. For each online peer it first requests `/api/servers/discovery` over HTTPS with a short per-peer timeout. A valid response is treated as the peer's RepoOS server list, and SSH is not invoked for that peer. If the endpoint cannot be reached or does not return the expected shape, the collector continues through the previous SSH commands. This preserves compatibility with installations that predate the endpoint.

The new endpoint returns only valid registered project names, ports, and the HTTPS authority used to reach the peer. It is separate from the signed-in Hub endpoint, so remote peer discovery does not require SSH credentials or a session cookie. The existing Hub route still uses `collectTailnetServers`, as does `repoos servers --tailscale`; consequently the transport fallback, failure reasons, peer filtering, and output rows remain centralized.

I expanded unsupported-device recognition to include OS values already known to be mobile, mobile-oriented Tailscale tags, and device names such as “Nothing Phone (3a)” when OS metadata is missing or inconsistent. This prevents a phone from becoming an SSH failure row just because Tailscale reports an unfamiliar OS string.

On the Hub discovery screen, project rows remain in the main results list. Rows marked unreachable move under a native collapsed disclosure labeled “Couldn't check these machines,” with the existing reason text retained. Saved and non-HTTPS project rows remain visible in the project list with their state notes. The target is to keep the outcome focused on RepoOS projects while preserving a useful explanation for failed peer checks.

The default whole-pass deadline is now twenty seconds instead of eight seconds. Peer checks remain parallel, and each HTTP attempt has its own short timeout before compatibility fallback. This avoids making the former eight-second aggregate budget the typical source of “timed out” failures when multiple peers are being checked concurrently.

## Approaches tried

The existing implementation already had a useful boundary: Tailscale parsing, URL annotation, and remote failure classification lived in `src/core/tailnet-servers.ts`. I extended that path rather than adding a mobile-specific network scanner or a second CLI discovery implementation. The peer endpoint shares the existing server registry as its source, and HTTP probing is injectable so the central path can be verified without a live tailnet.

An initial build caught two integration issues: the route module was already imported through the server route barrel, and the HTTP test seam had to be passed through `TailnetDiscoveryDeps` as well as the lower-level collector options. Both were corrected before continuing.

## Challenges and blockers

No live tailnet, phone, or real peer endpoints were available for this run. The endpoint and HTTP behavior are exercised using injected test responses; that does not establish that every machine on Nick’s tailnet has Tailscale Serve configured to expose the discovery path, nor that all projects on a machine have distinct HTTPS authorities. A real-device pass remains necessary to validate the acceptance scenario against actual Tailscale Serve configuration.

The CLI and Hub still receive specific SSH fallback reasons from the existing classifier. A compatibility peer that does not expose the new endpoint may still fail SSH, but that failure is kept as an unreachable result and the Hub now presents it in the collapsed machine-failure group.

## Key learnings

The peer list and the server discovery transport are separate concerns. Tailscale status gives stable machine identities, but SSH reachability from one machine does not imply SSH reachability from another. A peer-provided HTTPS endpoint avoids that key dependency while preserving SSH as a bridge for older installations.

Tests should focus on the transport decision: a fake successful HTTPS response must produce project rows and prove the SSH seam was not called. Device filtering also needs realistic display-name cases, because OS metadata alone does not cover every Tailscale client report. Finally, UI grouping can clarify a failure without changing the underlying shared response contract, which keeps the CLI and mobile consumers aligned.
